facts.text: Key Takeaways Reform as Survival Strategy, Not Substance: Iraq’s anti-corruption crackdown and militia disarmament deadline function less as coherent reform and more as a survival strategy for the Coordination Framework, aimed at satisfying Washington without confronting Iran-aligned power centers.

Compliance is already fractured: parliamentary-linked factions show partial willingness, while hardline, US-designated groups refuse outright, pointing toward an ambiguous outcome rather than real resolution.
A cosmetic disarmament process risks renewed attacks on US and Gulf targets and could trigger a fresh cycle of strikes on Iraqi soil.
Domestically, a weak coalition’s reliance on foreign-facing reform narratives, amid rising intra-Shia competition, threatens government stability.

Internationally, how Washington reads Baghdad’s actions will shape sanctions policy and test whether Iraq can maintain sovereignty between the US and Iran — or become the next flashpoint between them.

Al-Zaidi, a political newcomer, emerged as the compromise candidate because his good ties with rival Framework leaders meant he triggered no vetoes from al-Sudani, al-Maliki, or Chief Justice Faiq Zidan.

1 In parallel, Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for all armed factions to surrender weapons to state control, timed explicitly to coincide with the withdrawal of the US-led anti-ISIS coalition.

Tom Barrack met Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Baghdad on June 16, 2026, where the two stressed the “complete disarmament and disbandment” of militia groups as part of a shared vision for the new government.

The visit, Barrack’s first to Iraq in his envoy role, also took him to Erbil for talks with Kurdish leaders, including KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, on advancing trade and energy investment and supporting the federal government.

The al-Zaidi Washington visit should be used to establish concrete, monitorable benchmarks, such as verified weapons handover and PMF payroll transparency, rather than accepting rhetorical commitments as sufficient.

This should also include clarity on what happens to fighters and weapons after surrender, whether through integration into the Iraqi Security Forces, formal demobilization, or structured payout schemes, since the absence of such a pathway is likely to undermine compliance in practice.

It is the outcome of two decades of institutional erosion, sectarian bargaining, and external patronage, layered slowly enough that each step seemed manageable even as the cumulative effect reshaped the state itself.
Reversing that trajectory will not be accomplished through a single disarmament deadline, a single high-profile visit, or a single change of government.
It will require the same patience, consistency, and long-term investment that allowed the problem to take root in the first place.

Those seeking a sovereign, stable Iraq, in Baghdad and in Washington alike, should measure progress not by the speed of announcements, but by the durability of the institutions being rebuilt in their place.
Analysts note the real test begins now that he’s back in Baghdad, with any gains remaining “opportunities rather than guarantees.” 9
Three dynamics stand out for decision-makers:
This engagement should be paired with close monitoring of cross-border security risks, particularly given prior incidents linking Iraq-based groups to attacks on Gulf infrastructure.

Independent verification mechanisms for both the anti-corruption and disarmament processes are needed, given the credibility gap that regional analysts have identified between government messaging and actual enforcement patterns.
Iraq marks national ‘Sovereignty Days’ as US troops depart, but must navigate risks of new security landscape.
“But in reality, there is a great deal of concern that Iraq could be the next theatre of some major regional development,” he told Al Jazeera.
How the Iraqi government navigates the end of the US-led coalition’s deployment, dubbed “Operation Inherent Resolve”, will have wide-ranging implications for the future security of Iraq.
The country has remained relatively stable in recent years following the 2017 territorial defeat of ISIL, despite being enveloped by conflict and insecurity on its borders.

In the wake of the withdrawal, the two countries appear to be reverting to a 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, signed under the administration of US President George W Bush, Salih said.
The deal pledges continued, if non-binding, US security support for Iraq.
“There are real capabilities and real experience in the Iraqi security forces.
People I talk to in the military are quite confident that they can take on most threats against the sovereignty of Iraq,” former Ambassador Silliman said.

Hamzeh Hadad, an adjunct fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security, said there were no immediate signs the US planned a wholesale shift in its approach towards Iraq, which still houses the largest US embassy in the world in Baghdad and the largest consulate in Erbil.

Indeed, the US withdrawal appears to be part of a strategy by al-Zaidi to “politically weaken” influential militias , including those linked to Iran, according to Douglas Silliman, the former US ambassador to Iraq and Kuwait.

“This is one area where there will be vulnerabilities because it is clear that the pro-Iran militias have been willing to use drones and rockets and missiles against Iraqi targets inside Iraq, and as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that,” he said.
Speaking at the UNGA, al-Zaidi promised an economic “renaissance”, pledging to boost Iraq’s petrochemical industry and build new fossil fuel delivery routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
“Washington cannot dictate Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, nor can Tehran dictate Iraq’s relationship with Washington,” she said.
“What Iraq instead needs is the space to find its own balance.”
For his part, during a meeting at the White House in July, US PresidentTrump pledged “a lot of deals” to come with Iraq, pointing to the country’s vast oil reserves.
